zh.q: 一座氯碱厂，为什么同时送出烧碱、氯气和氢气？
zh.concl: 一套电解装置同时产三样：Cl₂、H₂、NaOH。原料只有食盐和水，难的是把产物分开、又保住效率——那正是中间那层膜要做的事。
points: 一套装置给三样产品：阴极得 H₂ 和 NaOH，阳极得 Cl₂，所以氯碱厂天然是「三合一」。
精制（①）只做一件事：把盐水里的钙镁洗掉，替②的膜挡掉结垢。
氯气（③）、氢气（④）、烧碱（⑤）是电解之后三条并联的产品线，不是串联。

zh.q: 原料只是食盐和水，为什么进槽前要先把盐水洗一遍？
zh.concl: Ca²⁺、Mg²⁺ 进膜后生成 Ca(OH)₂、Mg(OH)₂ 沉积在靠阴极的羧酸层里：电流效率下降、槽电压上升，损伤不可逆。
points: 一次精制用化学沉淀 + 过滤，把 Ca²⁺+Mg²⁺ 降到 ≤ 5 mg/L。
离子膜要求更高：再过螯合树脂塔做二次精制，降到 ≤ 20 μg/L。
只有两条硬约束：Na₂CO₃ 必须在 BaCl₂ 之后（顺带沉淀过量 Ba²⁺）、盐酸必须在过滤之后（否则沉淀又溶回去）；NaOH 加在哪一步是工艺选择。

zh.q: 一层膜夹在两块电极板中间，它到底把什么分开？
zh.concl: 两块电极各管一半：+x 侧 Cl⁻ 放电出 Cl₂，−x 侧水得电子出 H₂ 和 OH⁻；膜把两室隔开，产物才不会互相串。
points: 阳极是钛基涂钌铱：催化层让 Cl⁻ 优先放电、把水的析氧压住，否则氯气纯度下降、阳极被腐蚀。
阴极是镍基活性涂层：降低析氢过电位，水得电子生成 H₂ 和 OH⁻。
阴极得电子的是水，不是 Na⁺——水溶液里 Na⁺ 不放电，电解熔融 NaCl 才得到金属钠。

zh.q: 离子交换膜让什么通过、又把什么挡回去？
zh.concl: 固定负电荷排斥阴离子，只放 Na⁺ 带水通过：挡 Cl⁻ 保住烧碱纯度，挡 OH⁻ 保住电流效率。
points: 膜是多层复合膜：靠阳极的磺酸层厚、电阻低，管的是槽电压。
靠阴极的羧酸层薄、排斥 OH⁻，管的是电流效率——这一层做不好，效率就到不了实用水平。
Na⁺ 从一个固定负电荷跳到下一个，同时带大量水过去；所以阴极室要持续补纯水，把碱维持在 32 % 左右。

zh.q: 想让这座厂多产烧碱，把电流密度加大就行吗？
zh.concl: 产量随电流密度成正比涨，吨碱电耗也随槽电压线性涨；两者一起涨，才有「折中」这道题。
points: 产量与电流密度成正比，槽电压只是线性上升——斜率固定、截距 2.19 V 不为零。
所以电耗涨得比产量慢，但绝对值确实在涨：多产碱一定要多付电费。
手册的分级：3.5–4.5 kA/m² 属中电流密度，4.5–6.0 属高，超过 6.0 叫超高，槽与膜都吃力。

zh.q: 槽温只差几度，为什么也算进成本？
zh.concl: 槽温经槽电压直接影响电耗：90 ℃ 是工业标准温度，降到 85 ℃ 时每吨碱要多付 305 kW·h（2187 → 2492 kW·h/t）。
points: 槽温升高，膜里离子迁移更容易、电阻变小，槽电压与吨碱电耗一起下降。
但槽温不是越高越好：碱浓度会掉、膜效率有最佳峰值、氯气含水与设备腐蚀都加重。
所以工业把槽温稳在 90 ℃ 左右，本课的考核步也把槽温锁在 90 ℃。

zh.q: 把这层膜抽掉，槽里会发生什么？
zh.concl: 没有膜，Cl₂ 与 NaOH 反应把烧碱污染，H₂ 与 Cl₂ 也混到了一起；膜的第二个身份是安全屏障。
points: ① 氯气被碱吸收：教材写法（常温）是 Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O；90 ℃、32 % 的热浓碱主要生成氯酸钠——烧碱被污染、氯气白损失。
② OH⁻ 反渗到阳极室，抬高阳极液 pH，促生成 HClO / ClO₃⁻，腐蚀阳极、拉低氯气纯度。
H₂ 与 Cl₂ 混在同一空间，在一定组成与条件下受光照、火花等引发才可能爆炸——不是一见光就炸。现实靠氯中含氢分析 + 联锁停车防这一条。

zh.q: 产量和电耗同时卡死时，你调哪一个？
zh.concl: 只有 3.1–3.8 kA/m² 同时满足两个约束（3.0 只有 27.55 t/d，3.9 已 2303.8 kW·h/t）——折中是算出来的，不是背出来的。
points: 产量随电流密度成正比涨，电耗也跟着涨，两条线一起看才能在操作带里活下去。
电耗这条线把上界压到 3.88 kA/m²：3.9 已经是 2303.8 kW·h/t，超了。
1.0 kA/m² 电耗最低（1740 kW·h/t），但产碱只有 9.18 t/d，设备投资摊不回来——所以工厂不用它。
越过 6.5 kA/m² 会走「3 s 倒计时 → 穿膜 → 事故 → 复盘 → 抢修」，这条链要看懂。

en.q: Why does one chlor-alkali plant ship out caustic soda, chlorine and hydrogen all at once?
en.concl: One electrolysis unit makes three things at once: Cl₂, H₂ and NaOH. The raw materials are just salt and water; the hard part is separating the products while keeping efficiency, which is the job of the membrane in the middle.
points: One unit gives three products: H₂ and NaOH at the cathode, Cl₂ at the anode, so a chlor-alkali plant is naturally "three in one".
Purification (①) does one thing: washes calcium and magnesium out of the brine to keep scale out of the membrane in ②.
Chlorine (③), hydrogen (④) and caustic soda (⑤) are three parallel product lines after electrolysis, not a series.

en.q: The raw materials are just salt and water, so why must the brine be cleaned before entering the cell?
en.concl: Once Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ enter the membrane they form Ca(OH)₂ and Mg(OH)₂ deposits in the carboxylate layer on the cathode side: current efficiency falls and cell voltage rises, and the damage is irreversible.
points: Primary purification uses chemical precipitation + filtration to bring Ca²⁺+Mg²⁺ down to ≤ 5 mg/L.
The ion membrane demands more: a chelating resin tower does secondary purification down to ≤ 20 μg/L.

There are only two hard constraints: Na₂CO₃ must come after BaCl₂ (to precipitate excess Ba²⁺ as well), and HCl must come after filtration (or the precipitate redissolves); where NaOH is added is a process choice.

en.q: A membrane sits between two electrode plates: what exactly does it separate?
en.concl: Each electrode handles half: on the +x side Cl⁻ discharges to Cl₂, on the −x side water gains electrons to give H₂ and OH⁻; the membrane separates the chambers so the products don't mix.
points: The anode is titanium coated with ruthenium/iridium: the catalytic layer lets Cl⁻ discharge first and suppresses oxygen evolution from water; otherwise chlorine purity drops and the anode corrodes.
The cathode has a nickel-based active coating that lowers the hydrogen overpotential; water gains electrons to form H₂ and OH⁻.
It's water, not Na⁺, that gains electrons at the cathode; Na⁺ doesn't discharge in aqueous solution, and sodium metal is only obtained by electrolyzing molten NaCl.

en.q: What does the ion-exchange membrane let through, and what does it turn back?
en.concl: Fixed negative charges repel anions and let only Na⁺ through with water: blocking Cl⁻ keeps the caustic pure, blocking OH⁻ keeps the current efficiency up.
points: The membrane is a multilayer composite: the sulfonate layer on the anode side is thick and low-resistance, governing cell voltage.
The carboxylate layer on the cathode side is thin and repels OH⁻, governing current efficiency; if this layer isn't right, efficiency can't reach practical levels.
Na⁺ hops from one fixed negative charge to the next, carrying a lot of water with it, so the cathode chamber needs a steady supply of pure water to hold the caustic around 32 %.

en.q: To make more caustic soda, is it enough to raise the current density?
en.concl: Output rises in proportion to current density, and power per tonne rises linearly with cell voltage; both rise together, which is why there's a "trade-off" question.
points: Output is proportional to current density, while cell voltage only rises linearly: the slope is fixed and the 2.19 V intercept isn't zero.
So power use rises more slowly than output, but it does rise in absolute terms: more caustic always costs more electricity.
Handbook classes: 3.5–4.5 kA/m² is medium current density, 4.5–6.0 is high, above 6.0 is ultra-high, which strains both cell and membrane.

en.q: Why do just a few degrees of cell temperature count in the cost?
en.concl: Cell temperature affects power use directly through cell voltage: 90 ℃ is the industrial standard, and at 85 ℃ each tonne of caustic costs 305 kW·h more (2187 → 2492 kW·h/t).
points: Higher cell temperature makes ion migration in the membrane easier and resistance lower, so cell voltage and power per tonne both fall.
But hotter isn't always better: caustic concentration drops, membrane efficiency has an optimum peak, and moisture in chlorine and equipment corrosion get worse.
So industry holds the cell at about 90 ℃, and this lesson's assessment step also locks it at 90 ℃.

en.q: Pull this membrane out: what happens in the cell?
en.concl: Without the membrane, Cl₂ reacts with NaOH and contaminates the caustic, and H₂ and Cl₂ mix; the membrane's second role is a safety barrier.
points: ① Chlorine is absorbed by the caustic: the textbook form (room temperature) is Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O; hot concentrated 32 % caustic at 90 ℃ mainly forms sodium chlorate; the caustic is contaminated and chlorine is wasted.
② OH⁻ back-migrates into the anode chamber, raising the anolyte pH and promoting HClO / ClO₃⁻, which corrode the anode and lower chlorine purity.

H₂ and Cl₂ in the same space can explode only at certain compositions and conditions when triggered by light, sparks and so on, not on any exposure to light. In practice, hydrogen-in-chlorine analysis + interlock shutdown guards against this.

en.q: When output and power use are both constrained, which do you adjust?
en.concl: Only 3.1–3.8 kA/m² satisfies both constraints (3.0 gives only 27.55 t/d, 3.9 is already 2303.8 kW·h/t); the compromise is calculated, not memorized.
points: Output rises in proportion to current density and power use follows; only by watching both lines can you survive in the operating band.
The power line caps the upper bound at 3.88 kA/m²: 3.9 is already 2303.8 kW·h/t, over the limit.
1.0 kA/m² has the lowest power use (1740 kW·h/t), but output is only 9.18 t/d and the equipment investment can't be recovered, so plants don't use it.
Going past 6.5 kA/m² triggers "3 s countdown → membrane breach → accident → review → repair"; understand this chain.
